name: Yemsa
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 1 other work consulted does not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Zaugg-Coretti, Silvia. 2013. The Verbal System of Yemsa (Omotic language of Ethiopia). PhD dissertation, University of Zurich, Faculty of Arts (accepted 2010, printed 2013). 368 pp. DOI 10.5167/uzh-87425 (ZORA open repository).
catalog_locator: §2.5 'Stress', p. 53; §2.6 'Tone' opens on the same page (pp. 53-72); verb wu 'say' remark p. 112.
catalog_quote: I am unable to provide a detailed description of stress in Yemsa. Lamberti (1993:59f) states that stress is primarily on one of the syllables of the stem, though it can be on the suffix if it carries high tone. However, he does not state how stress is manifested. Lamberti (1993) is basically right. On two-syllable words with the same tone on both syllables the first syllable, i.e. the root, is pronounced with more power. If an ensuing syllable, i.e. the stem vowel or a suffix, carries a higher tone than the root, this gives the impression of stress, and indeed, such a syllable is pronounced with more power than a stem vowel syllable with a lower tone. Nevertheless, this can be a natural effect of the high tone. ... First, on one-syllable words with the CV syllable pattern, the vowel is regularly lengthened as a result of stress. Thus, e.g. /dà/ 'ground, country' and /fō/ 'life, wealth' are pronounced [daː] and [foː] respectively. ... The second observation concerns two-syllable suffixes with low tone like -fènì (IPFV 1p/2POL) or -bèsì (3pPOSS). There, the low tone of the first syllable is slightly higher than the one of the last syllable, but not as high as a preceding mid. This behaviour is considered as another, tonal, manifestation of stress. [§2.6 Tone:] Yemsa is characterised by a tonal system with three level tones: low, mid and high. In addition there is a rising tone, depending on the neighbouring tones realised as low-high or mid-high.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Yemsa is a tone language (three level tones L/M/H plus a rising tone; §2.6). Word stress is weak and not fully described: by default it falls on the root, i.e. the first syllable of a disyllabic word when both syllables carry the same tone; a later syllable (stem vowel or suffix) that carries a higher tone than the root is pronounced with more force and is perceived as stressed, which may simply be an effect of high tone. Phonetic correlates: CV monosyllables lengthen the vowel under stress (/da/ [da:], /fo/ [fo:], also before suffixes: [da:-k]); in disyllabic low-tone suffixes the first syllable is slightly raised.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned. The only remark on suffix-internal prominence: in two-syllable low-tone suffixes (-feni, -besi) the first syllable is slightly higher than the second, 'considered as another, tonal, manifestation of stress'.
new_statements.exceptions: Pronouns like ne 'you' may have long or short vowel depending on emphasis; the verb wu 'say' never lengthens its vowel, 'possible reason.. is that this verb is never stressed' as it co-occurs with another verb of saying (p. 187 of text; ch. on irregular verbs). The author states explicitly that she cannot give a detailed description and that the apparent suffix stress may be just high tone.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (root/stem vs. suffix), described on isolated word forms and in running text; no phrase-level stress statement. Author's own field data (Sokoru, Addis Ababa, Karateya/Yengar, 2006-2009), building on Lamberti 1993:59f.
new_statements.identity_note: Yemsa proper (yems1235, ISO jnj), data from Sokoru, Addis Ababa and the village of Karateya in Yengar (Yem Special Wereda), 2006-2009. Zaugg-Coretti 2013:35 states Yemsa 'does not show significant internal variation'; the only slightly divergent dialect is Toba (Aklilu Yilma & Siebert 2002), not separately coded in Glottolog. Lamberti 1993 (the source of the endorsed stress rule) is the same language under the same name.
